resources.string: Picture patterns (%1$d), Left and Right change pattern
%1$d of %2$d, %3$s levels, %4$d x %5$d px. Left/Right: pattern. Up/Down: limited or full levels. OK: hide this help. Back: exit.
START WITH THE VOLUME LOW. Signals peak at -12 dBFS and fade in, but a test tone can still be loud.
Press OK to play again, Back to leave.
Equal energy in every octave, for a microphone or your ear. A speaker with a flat response sounds even, neither boomy nor thin.
EQ bands: 125 Hz to 8 kHz, 4 s each
Seven tones, 125, 250, 500 Hz, 1, 2, 4 and 8 kHz, four seconds each with a second of silence: the TV equaliser\'s own bands. Record them and run tools/calibrate_sound.py.
Listen for rattles, buzzes and dips; the bass drops out below what the speakers can reach.
A smooth rise from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Listen for rattles and buzzes in the cabinet, and for where the bass starts and the treble ends.
A 1 kHz beep on the left, then on the right, three times. Each should come from its own side; if they swap, the speaker wires or the TV setting are crossed.

Brightness. Background is 16, video black. Bars read 0 to 25. Lower Brightness until the bars at 0 to 14 vanish into the background, then raise it until 18 and above only just show. Bars below 16 should never be visible; 18 should be a faint step.

Brightness for full-range signals. Background is 0. Raise Brightness until bar 1 or 2 just shows, lower it until bar 0 and the background cannot be told apart. If bars up to 8 are invisible, shadows are being crushed; check the HDMI range.

Contrast. Lower Contrast (or the Local Contrast, Adaptive Luma or Dynamic Contrast settings) until you can tell every bar from its neighbours. In limited range 235 is white; bars from 236 up show only when the TV passes super-whites. If several bars merge, the highlights are clipped.

Top: every grey code, no banding in a good picture. Bottom: 0 to 100 percent in tens. Each step should be a little lighter than the one before and nothing should have a colour tint; a tint means white balance is off. Visible stripes on the ramp mean banding or a processing setting.

White, yellow, cyan, green, magenta, red, blue, then a grey scale. Colour should be rich but not glowing. Use the colour filter (blue only) if your TV has one, and match the blue bars. Skin tones in a film should not turn orange or green.

The same bars at full level. Every bar should have a distinct edge and the same brightness across its width. A bar that bleeds or loses detail is clipped or oversaturated, so lower Colour or turn off Vivid modes.

Each row grows from grey to the pure primary in steps of 20 percent. Look for steps that merge near the end (clipping) or skip (a colour gamut or boost setting). Each step should look evenly stronger than the last.

The same for the secondary colours. Yellow and cyan are bright, magenta darker; a hue shift along the row (yellow going green or orange) points at the colour management or a colour temperature that is too cool or too warm.

Left and middle: 1-pixel lines, right: a checkerboard. Turn Sharpness down until there are no bright halos or ringing beside edges; the lines should be uniform. The border on the edge of the screen must be visible on all four sides, otherwise turn overscan off (Just Scan, Full Pixel or Screen Fit). The circle should be round.

Step back and squint. Each column shows a fine black and white checkerboard with a solid square calibrated for a gamma of 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.4 and 2.6. The square that disappears into the checkerboard is your TV\'s gamma. Aim for 2.2 in a bright room, 2.4 in the dark.

Dark scenes. Look for clouding, bright corners or a vertical band across the screen. Turn the room lights down and ignore reflections. A little variation is normal; a patch that is clearly lighter is panel or backlight.
The best test for dirty screen effect and colour tint. The field should be one even grey with no tint of green or magenta and no darker edges or centre.
Look for yellowing, cool edges, dark corners or banding. If the white looks too bright to look at in a dark room, lower the backlight (not Contrast).
Full-screen red. Look for dead or stuck pixels (black or white dots), darker areas and colour patches.
Full-screen green. Look for dead or stuck pixels, darker areas and colour patches.
Full-screen blue. Look for dead or stuck pixels, darker areas and colour patches.

A white square, a still square, moving stripes and text cross the screen at the same speed. With motion smoothing (MEMC) off, edges should be sharp and move in small steps. Turn it up until the text stays readable without the soap-opera look, halos behind the square or tearing of the stripes. Low is usually enough.
